newsitem.title: UK: Skids to stay under oil as price hits 12-month low.
newsitem.headline: Skids to stay under oil as price hits 12-month low.

text.p: World oil prices on Monday were hovering near 12-month lows as traders decided that seasonal demand for gasoline in the West was falling below expectations.
And analysts said prices over the next few months would struggle to resume the rally which took crude to six-year highs last winter.
"The pressure on prices remains downward," said Geoff Pyne at Swiss finance house UBS. "There's nothing positive the market can cling on to at the moment."
Speculative investment funds cashed in their chips on crude futures exchanges in New York and London on Friday, helping push prices close to their lowest levels since June last year.
London July futures for benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude on Monday were down six cents at $17.65 a barrel on top of a 62 cent slide on Friday.
"The funds gave oil a second chance in May but now they seem to be washing their hands of it," said a futures trader in London.
"Stocks are up, supplies are comfortable and the gasoline season has ended before it even got started.

Brent has lost $3 in less than a month, and is $7 below January's high, amid a build in stocks of motor fuel in the gasoline-greedy United States. Cool spring weather across the country has stemmed demand from casual drivers.
Traders and analysts said worldwide demand for crude oil, though rising strongly, had proved no match so far this year for the growth in extra supplies.
"Demand is strong but it's just not strong enough," said Pyne. "I don't see any reason why the market should go back up in the next three to six months."
Russell Hill, senior trader at Austrian oil company OMV said he had pencilled $15-$18 Brent into projections for the remainder of the year.
Renewal last week by the United Nations of its humanitarian oil deal with Iraq will swell supplies when exports from Baghdad resume in a few weeks.
At lower world prices than in the first six months of the arrangement, Iraq would have to export larger volumes to meet the $2 billion of sales allowed under U.N. terms.
Current low oil prices come just two weeks ahead of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries' (OPEC) summer ministerial conference.
The cartel, widely expected to leave production quotas unchanged for the second half of the year, nevertheless continues to pump rising supplies as most members ignore their official allocations.
Estimates put OPEC output in recent months not far below 27 million barrels a day (bpd) nearly two million bpd in excess of its combined official ceiling.
